subject: History
source: National Curriculum KS2 (Britain's settlement by Anglo-Saxons and Scots; the Viking and Anglo-Saxon struggle for the Kingdom of England); no school Drive history material found for Y5, written from scratch

lessons.title: The Anglo-Saxons arrive
objectives: Explain why the Anglo-Saxons came to Britain
Locate the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms on a map

keywords.def: people from the Angles, Saxons and Jutes who settled in Britain
to make a home in a new place
a land ruled by a king or queen
moving from one place to live in another

starter: Around which year did the Romans leave Britain?
What does the word legacy mean?

teach.heading: Bismillah: after the Romans
bullets: Roman rule ended around AD 410
Britain faced attacks from raiders
Settlers came across the North Sea
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Recap Year 4 learning on the Romans. Ask: what might happen to a country when its army leaves? Collect ideas.

teach.heading: Who were they?
bullets: The Angles, Saxons and Jutes
They came from Denmark and northern Germany
They sailed in wooden boats
teach.note: The Angles gave England its name (Angle-land). Use a map to show the sea crossing. Explain that Anglo-Saxon settlement happened gradually, over many years, in the fifth and sixth centuries.

teach.heading: Why did they come?
bullets: They wanted better farmland
Their homes flooded or were crowded
Some may have been invited as soldiers
teach.note: Historians suggest several reasons. Stress we cannot be certain: our evidence is limited because few written records survive. Link to why people migrate today.

teach.heading: Seven kingdoms
bullets: Britain divided into small kingdoms
Kingdoms included Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria
Kings often fought each other
teach.note: Show a map of the main kingdoms: Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, Wessex. Mention the old name 'Heptarchy'. Ask pupils where they live and which kingdom it was.

practice: Where did the Anglo-Saxons come from?
Name two reasons they came to Britain.
independent: Label a map of Anglo-Saxon England with six kingdoms
Draw arrows showing where the Angles, Saxons and Jutes came from
Write a paragraph beginning 'The Anglo-Saxons came to Britain because ...'
exit: Which group gave England its name?
lessons.homework: Find out where the name of your area or nearby town comes from; some end in -ham, -ton or -ley from Old English.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-labelled map to colour and a word bank. Stretch: explain why historians find it hard to be sure why the Anglo-Saxons came.

lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon life, Sutton Hoo and Christianity
objectives: Describe life in an Anglo-Saxon village
Explain what Sutton Hoo tells us about Anglo-Saxon society

keywords.def: a nobleman who served the king
a site in Suffolk with a royal ship burial
studying the past through objects and sites
a person sent to spread a religion

starter: Which three groups made up the Anglo-Saxons?
Why does moving house or country happen?

teach.heading: Village life
bullets: Villages had wooden halls and small huts
Most people were farmers
Families made clothes, tools and pots
teach.note: Show a reconstruction of West Stow village. Compare Roman towns with Anglo-Saxon villages. Misconception: Anglo-Saxons were less skilled; they made fine metalwork and jewellery.

teach.heading: Sutton Hoo
bullets: Found in Suffolk in 1939
A ship burial of a king, probably Raedwald
It held gold, silver and a helmet
teach.note: Sutton Hoo is dated to around AD 625 and the person is usually thought to be King Raedwald of East Anglia. Say 'probably'. Show the helmet. The ship had rotted, leaving an impression in the sand.

teach.heading: What the evidence shows
bullets: Rich objects came from far away
The king had power and trade links
It challenges the idea of a 'dark age'
teach.note: Garnets from India or Sri Lanka and silver from the Byzantine Empire were found. Ask what this suggests about contact with the wider world, including the Muslim world later, through trade.

teach.heading: Christianity arrives
bullets: Pope Gregory sent Augustine in AD 597
Augustine met King Ethelbert in Kent
Monasteries copied books by hand
teach.note: Keep to the facts. Anglo-Saxons had earlier followed pagan gods like Woden and Thor, remembered in Wednesday and Thursday. Treat all religions respectfully.

practice: What was found at Sutton Hoo?
Why is the ship burial important to historians?
What was a monastery used for?
independent: Draw an Anglo-Saxon village with labels
Write a museum label for the Sutton Hoo helmet
Explain what Sutton Hoo tells us about the king in 5 sentences
exit: Name two things found in the Sutton Hoo burial.
Who brought Christianity to Kent in AD 597?
lessons.homework: Find out which day of the week is named after an Anglo-Saxon god and write the name of the god.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: museum label starters and a picture bank. Stretch: say what is still unknown about Sutton Hoo.

lessons.title: Viking raiders
objectives: Explain who the Vikings were and where they came from
Describe the Viking raid on Lindisfarne in AD 793

keywords.def: a seafaring people from Scandinavia who raided and settled lands
the region of Norway, Sweden and Denmark
a long, narrow Viking boat with oars and a sail
a community of monks who live and pray together

starter: Name a famous Anglo-Saxon burial site.
Who brought Christianity to Kent in AD 597?
Which kingdom was Sutton Hoo in?

teach.heading: Who were the Vikings?
bullets: Vikings came from Norway, Sweden and Denmark
They were farmers, traders and raiders
Their boats let them cross seas quickly
teach.note: Bismillah. Challenge the stereotype that Vikings were only raiders with horned helmets; there is no evidence they wore horned helmets. Show a longship picture.

teach.heading: Why leave home?
bullets: Land in Scandinavia was scarce
Rich monasteries could be raided
Viking kings wanted power and wealth
teach.note: Use 'historians suggest'. Ask pupils to rank reasons: which seems most convincing? Link to migration reasons last lesson.

teach.heading: Lindisfarne, AD 793
bullets: Vikings attacked a monastery on Lindisfarne
It is an island off Northumbria
Monks were killed and treasure was stolen
teach.note: This is the first well-known Viking raid, recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Remember the Chronicle was written by monks, so sources could be biased. Show the island on a map.

teach.heading: Raiders become settlers
bullets: Raids grew bigger across the 800s
In AD 865 a 'Great Army' arrived
Vikings began to settle and farm
teach.note: Explain the shift from raiding to settlement. Pupils should note not all Vikings were violent; many traded peacefully. Include Viking trade routes reaching Baghdad, where silver coins were exchanged (link to Year 6).

practice: Where did the Vikings come from?
Why might the monks' accounts be one-sided?
independent: Draw and label a Viking longship
Write a newspaper report: 'Raid on Lindisfarne, AD 793'
Make a mind map of reasons the Vikings came to Britain
exit: What happened at Lindisfarne in AD 793?
Give one reason why a monk's account might be biased.
lessons.homework: Find three Viking words in English (e.g. sky, egg, knife) and note their meanings.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: newspaper template with headline word bank. Stretch: compare two reasons for Viking raids and say which is stronger.

lessons.title: Alfred the Great and the Danelaw
objectives: Explain how Alfred of Wessex resisted the Vikings

keywords.def: the part of England ruled by the Vikings under their law
a formal agreement between two sides
the Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the south of England

starter: What does a longship look like?

teach.heading: Vikings take land
bullets: By AD 870 the Vikings controlled most kingdoms
Only Wessex remained
Alfred became king in AD 871
teach.note: Bismillah. Point out Northumbria, East Anglia and most of Mercia fell. Alfred was the youngest brother; ask pupils how it feels to lead in a crisis.

teach.heading: Battle of Edington
bullets: In AD 878 Alfred beat the Viking leader Guthrum
Guthrum agreed to be baptised
Alfred kept Wessex safe
teach.note: Mention the story of Alfred and the cakes is a legend, not proven fact. Ask: why is it useful to tell legends from evidence?

teach.heading: The Danelaw
bullets: A treaty divided England
Vikings ruled the north and east
Alfred ruled the south and west
teach.note: Show the line on a map. 'Dane law' means areas where Viking law applied. Place names ending in -by and -thorpe show Viking settlement.

teach.heading: Alfred's reforms
bullets: He built burhs, fortified towns
He built ships and organised an army
He encouraged learning and laws
teach.note: Alfred valued education and had books translated into English. Link to the idea in Islam of seeking knowledge. Alfred died in AD 899; his grandson Athelstan became the first king of all England in AD 927.

practice: Which place-name endings show Viking influence?
independent: Colour a map of England showing the Danelaw and Wessex
Write a short profile of Alfred explaining why he is called 'the Great'
List three things you would do to defend a town from raiders
exit: Which battle did Alfred win in AD 878?
Give one reason Alfred is called 'the Great'.
lessons.homework: Find a place near you or in England that ends in -by or -thorpe and say what you think it means.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn map outline with key words to attach. Stretch: judge whether Alfred deserved the title 'the Great' using three pieces of evidence.
